The 12th report of the Shanghai Mission to Rikisha men states:—
If in some former years the happy monotony of the peaceful routine of the Mission's work has tended to a measure of repetition in the annual report, this year, with its attendant political and social upheavals and unrest, has provided a sufficiency of alarms and menaces to the peace and safety of the work to provide quite sensational writing if considered desirable, but having weathered all successfully, it seems more fitting to dwell gratefully on what has been avoided.

label: text
text: In the early Spring of 1925 life was very hard for the majority of rikisha men and their class, and needless to say, the warm, brightly lighted Mission halls, where food, clothing, and shelter by day and night could be obtained by destitute men, were very popular resorts, and the Mission workers had hard work to meet all the requirements of the relief work, in the Mission and outside.

label: text
text:
During this troubled year there has been no decrease in the numbers passing through the Mission premises and attending the daily and nightly gathering in open air, and in the halls. Even during the disturbances, the usual large crowds. (In which representatives from most of the provinces might be found) were always present, orderly and friendly in attitude. The usual routine was carried on uninterruptedly. Sick and injured men were sent to hospital and the destitute were relieved as usual.
The homes, shelters and other places of resort have been visited regularly and assistance given where needed.

label: text
text: In visiting and open air work large numbers of men, women, and children are reached who would otherwise remain unknown, and in the course of this itinerant work large quantities of suitable literature are distributed, including Scripture portions and leaflets, Health Department Instructions and Municipal and Police Regulations etc.

label: text
text:
A day memorable in the history of Shanghai is the beginning of the general strike which most seriously affected all the industrial sections of the city for over three months except the rikisha pullers who alone stood untouched by the strike movement, although most determined efforts were made to induce the men to stop work.
Strike promoters tried all methods at their command to attain their aim, intimidation, actual violence, inflammatory literature, promises of money and support, etc., but all failed. The rikisha man refused to be threatened pra cajoled.

label: text
text:
To counteract the pernicious efforts of the agitators, the Mission staff under the direct supervision of the Hon. Director Mr. George Matheson, worked unceasingly during the strike, addressing great crowds in the Mission halls, open air, lodging and tea houses and homes, urging the preservation of law and order, and distributing "the Municipal Council's propaganda leaflets," "Read the Truth," "of which about 24,000 were circulated by the Mission staff along with an abridged account of twelve years work of the Rikisha Mission, which it was hoped might convey a favourable impression of the good feeling towards Chinese on the part of the foreign community.
The counter propaganda work was attended by considerable risk to the distributers who were threatened with violence by the strike promoters, but happily it had the desired effect, for the rikisha men stuck cheerfully and manfully to their shafts, thereby earning the gratitude of many foreigners to whom the absence of rikisha would have been a great inconvenience. The general opinion of the public during the strike was that "the conduct of the men was admirable, in consideration of which the majority of foreign users of rikisha treated them with sympathetic kindness.

label: text
text: The long-talked-of and urgently needed new building has assumed a more solid aspect in-as-much as that May 19, 1925, saw the completion of the purchase of Lob No. R.C. 11252, as a site for the new Mission premises.

label: text

label: text
text:
Scotland Yards flying squad will probably soon stamp out robbery by motor-car in the metro-politan area, but the use of these vehicles in other parts of the country is naturally causing considerable concern.
Nowadays, when everyone motors, there is nothing unusual in cars being seen in out-of-the-way places, and it is obviously impossible for the police to challenge everyone they meet. Standardisation and mass production have robbed cars of their distinctive appearance and as the registration number is the only thing "different" about the majority of cheap motors the task of identifying a particular vehicle is extremely difficult. And it is so easy to change the number plate and drive away under the noses of the police, hot though they be on the trail.
